title: Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests
subtitle: From a sample to a statement about the population — with an honest measure of how wrong we might be.

est.title: Estimation
est.body: A statistic computed from a sample estimates a population parameter: x̄ for μ, s² for σ² (÷(n − 1) makes it unbiased), p̂ for p. A good estimator is unbiased (right on average) and has small standard error σ/√n — more data tightens it.

ci.title: Confidence interval for a mean
ci.body: With σ known (or n large): x̄ ± z·σ/√n, where z = 1.645, 1.96, 2.576 for 90 %, 95 %, 99 %. The 95 % means: if you repeated the whole sampling many times, about 95 % of the intervals built this way would contain μ. It is not a 95 % chance that μ lies in one given interval. Below, 100 simulated intervals at z = 1.96 caught the true mean 96% of the time; at z = 2.576 99% (wider, half-width 5.152 vs 3.92).
ci.steps: n = 25, x̄ = 52, σ = 10. Standard error = 10/5. 95 % half-width = 1.96 × 2 = 3.92.

n.title: Effect of n and confidence level
n.body: Width = 2zσ/√n. Raising confidence raises z (wider). Raising n shrinks it: half-width is 3.92 at n = 25 but 1.96 at n = 100. Precision, confidence and cost pull against each other; you choose two.

ht.title: Hypothesis testing: the logic
ht.body: State a null hypothesis H₀ (“nothing special”, e.g. μ = μ₀) and an alternative H₁. Compute a test statistic, e.g. z = (x̄ − μ₀)/(σ/√n). If it falls in the rejection region (|z| > 1.96 at α = 0.05, two-sided) — equivalently if the p-value < α — reject H₀. Errors: Type I = rejecting a true H₀ (probability α); Type II = failing to reject a false H₀ (probability β; power = 1 − β).

ztest.title: Worked test of a mean
ztest.body: A maker claims a bulb lasts 1000 h (σ = 80). A sample of 64 averages 980 h. Is the claim still believable at α = 0.05?
ztest.steps: H₀: μ = 1000, H₁: μ ≠ 1000. SE = 80/√64. Test statistic. |z| = 2 exceeds 1.96, so reject H₀ (p ≈ 0.046).

t.title: Unknown σ: the t-test
t.body: When σ must be estimated by s, use t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n) with n − 1 degrees of freedom. The t distribution has heavier tails than the normal, so critical values are larger (2.262 at 9 d.f. vs 1.96) — the price of not knowing σ. As n grows, t → z. For two proportions or categorical counts the χ² test compares observed and expected counts: χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E.
